title: Domestication of the donkey
summary: The donkey was domesticated from the African wild ass about 6,000 years ago in north-east Africa, possibly by pastoralists coping with a drying Sahara; genetic work points to Nubian wild asses as ancestors of one main lineage. The earliest evidence of its use for transport comes from ten ass skeletons buried about 3000 BCE beside a royal mortuary complex at Abydos in Egypt, all with bone damage from carrying loads. Donkeys let herders move further with their households and helped the early Egyptian state move food in bulk.

uncertainty.note: Domestication is dated to ≈6,000 years ago in northeast Africa; articulated load-bearing skeletons at Abydos date to c. 3000 BCE.

as_recorded.calendar: Evolutionary history, mitochondrial and nuclear genomics

where.modern_name: Nile Valley and eastern Sahara; reference site at Abydos, Sohag Governorate, Egypt
where.historical_name: Upper Egypt and northeastern Africa (Predynastic to Early Dynastic periods); reference burials at Abdju (Abydos)

importance.justification: Gave Africa and Asia a desert-hardy pack animal, transforming pastoral life and early state transport (R3 D3 T4 L2).

beats.caption: African pastoralists domesticated the wild ass in northeastern Africa as drying conditions spread across the Sahara.
Donkeys became essential pack animals across Egyptian mortuary complexes and ancient Near Eastern caravan trade routes.
